title: Tense and aspect choices: cumulative review
objectives: Choose tense and aspect for a stated viewpoint.
Review perfect simple and continuous forms.

explanation.heading: Meaning and use
paragraphs: Tense locates a situation in relation to a point of reference; aspect presents it from a particular viewpoint, such as completed, ongoing or connected to another time. These choices help a reader follow a narrative or understand why a past action matters now. ‘I've repaired the door’ foregrounds a present result. ‘I've been repairing the door’ foregrounds the activity, which may or may not be complete.

This unit reviews present, past and future perfect forms alongside narrative forms. More than one form can be grammatical in many contexts. Instead of searching for one tense that always belongs with a time word, decide which time and aspect the speaker intends to highlight.

explanation.heading: Form
paragraphs: The present perfect simple is have or has plus a past participle; the continuous is have or has been plus -ing. A completed number often favours the simple: ‘I've answered six emails’. A duration or recent activity can favour the continuous: ‘I've been answering emails for an hour’. Both forms can describe an ongoing situation with some verbs: ‘I've lived here for years’ and ‘I've been living here for years’.

The past perfect simple is had plus a participle; the continuous is had been plus -ing. The simple can foreground an earlier result: ‘By noon, she had written three reports’. The continuous can foreground activity leading to a past point: ‘She had been writing for hours when the power failed’.

explanation.heading: Examples in context
paragraphs: The future continuous is will be plus -ing; the future perfect is will have plus a participle. ‘At ten tomorrow, I'll be meeting a client’ presents an activity in progress at a future point. ‘By ten, I'll have finished the report’ presents completion no later than that point. A simple future can also be appropriate in many situations: ‘I'll finish by ten’.

In a past narrative, the past simple commonly moves events forward: ‘I opened the door and stepped inside’. The past continuous can provide background: ‘Rain was falling as I entered’. The past perfect can identify an event earlier than the narrative reference point: ‘Someone had left a message before I arrived’.

explanation.heading: Contrasts and common mistakes
paragraphs: Do not assume the continuous proves an action is unfinished. ‘I've been painting’ focuses on the activity; the context may show that it has stopped or even finished. Nor does a duration such as for five years automatically demand a continuous form. State verbs such as know normally use the simple in their usual state meaning.

Avoid unnecessary past perfect forms when ordinary chronological order is already clear. ‘She stood up and left’ is a natural sequence. A sentence can permit several tense choices with different implications, so the exercises specify the intended viewpoint when a single answer is required.

examples.note: The simple foregrounds a completed number.

examples.sentence: I've been answering emails for an hour.
examples.note: The continuous foregrounds activity and duration.

examples.sentence: By noon, she had written three reports.
examples.note: The past perfect simple foregrounds an earlier completed amount.

examples.sentence: She had been writing for hours when the power failed.
examples.note: The continuous foregrounds activity before the past event.

examples.sentence: At ten tomorrow, I'll be meeting a client.
examples.note: The future continuous presents progress at a future point.

examples.sentence: By ten, I'll have finished the report.
examples.note: The future perfect presents completion by a future point.

examples.sentence: Rain was falling as I entered.
I opened the door and stepped inside.
examples.note: Past simple verbs move a sequence forward.

common_errors.incorrect: I have been knowing her for years.
common_errors.correct: I have known her for years.
common_errors.reason: Know normally uses the simple form in this state meaning.

common_errors.incorrect: They had been write for an hour.
common_errors.correct: They had been writing for an hour.
common_errors.reason: Use an -ing form after had been in this pattern.

common_errors.incorrect: She will have wrote it by noon.
common_errors.correct: She will have written it by noon.
common_errors.reason: Use the past participle written after will have.

summary: Choose aspect according to the intended reference point and focus.
Simple and continuous forms can overlap; context establishes whether a contrast matters.
Use past narrative forms to distinguish sequence, background and earlier events.

exercises.explanation: Has written presents the completed number.

option_feedback.c: “has been writing five emails for” does not fit here. Has written presents the completed number.
option_feedback.d: “has wrote” does not fit here. Has written presents the completed number.
